marks.gloss_en: מאי שנא מכאן ואילך מצות קריאה -- דכתיב לדבר בם? הכא נמי הא כתיב ודברת בם! -- if recitation is the mitzva only from 'upon your heart' on because 'to speak of them' is written there, the first paragraph has 'and you shall speak of them' too
הכי קאמר: עד כאן מצות כוונה וקריאה, מכאן ואילך קריאה בלא כוונה -- recitation runs throughout; what changes at 'upon your heart' is that intent stops (= p_rz_reading)
this is what Rav Zutra means: to here the mitzva of intent AND recitation; from here on, recitation without intent
ומאי שנא עד כאן מצות כוונה וקריאה דכתיב על לבבך ודברת בם? התם נמי הא כתיב על לבבכם לדבר בם! -- the second paragraph too has 'upon your heart', so intent should be required there as well

ההוא מבעי ליה לכדרבי יצחק -- the second paragraph's 'upon your heart' is needed for R' Yitzchak's teaching that the tefillin are placed opposite the heart (= p_sima_keneged_halev), so it does not teach intent
R' Yitzchak: 'and you shall place these words' -- the placing [of the tefillin] must be opposite the heart
R' Akiva: 'which I command you this day, upon your heart' -- from here you learn that the whole paragraph requires intent
Rabba bar bar Chana in R' Yochanan's name: the halakha follows R' Akiva
one who reads the Shema must focus his heart
Rav Zutra: 'upon your heart' -- to here the mitzva of intent, from here on the mitzva of recitation (the utterance; its law is the stam's construal at 13b.6)
ואזדא רבי יוחנן לטעמיה -- R' Yochanan follows his own reasoning, as shown by his ruling that the halakha follows R' Acha in R' Yehuda's name
Rabba bar bar Chana in R' Yochanan's name: the halakha follows R' Acha, who said it in R' Yehuda's name
Rav Yehuda (as transmitted): 'upon your heart' -- standing (the utterance; its law is fixed by the stam's emendation)
בשלמא לדידי דאמינא אינו חוזר וגומרה, היינו דמהדר רבי אשמעתא דאית בה יציאת מצרים -- granted for me: since he does not complete the Shema, that is why he seeks out a lesson with the Exodus
אלא לדידך דאמרת חוזר וגומרה, למה ליה לאהדורי? -- if Rebbi completes the Shema later, why does he seek out a lesson containing the Exodus?
R' Shimon beRabbi: he [Rebbi] goes back and completes it [the Shema]
כדי להזכיר יציאת מצרים בזמנה -- in order to mention the Exodus in its time (= p_lehazkir_yetziat_mitzrayim_bizmana)
[he seeks it out] in order to mention the Exodus in its time
מקרא הוא דלא ליקרי, הא מיגנא שפיר דמי? והא רבי יהושע בן לוי לייט אמאן דגני אפרקיד! -- Rav Yosef's wording implies sleeping on the back is fine, but R' Yehoshua ben Levi cursed it
Rav Yosef: one lying on his back shall not recite the Shema
אמרי: מיגנא כי מצלי שפיר דמי, מקרא אף על גב דמצלי נמי אסור -- sleeping is fine when leaning; reciting is forbidden even when leaning (= p_miyegna_ki_matzlei_shapir, p_mikra_afilu_matzlei_asur)
sleeping [on the back] when one leans [to the side] is fine
והא רבי יוחנן מצלי וקרי! -- but R' Yochanan would lean and recite
R' Yochanan would lean and recite
שאני רבי יוחנן דבעל בשר הוה -- R' Yochanan is different, for he was corpulent
the baraita: 'Hear, Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One' -- this is the Shema of R' Yehuda HaNasi
Rav: one who said 'Hear, Israel ... the Lord is One' and was overcome by sleep has fulfilled [his obligation]

(entertained) R' Meir's 'and responds' at the breaks is out of respect -- rejected at 13b.27 as needless (if he may greet out of respect, surely he may respond), reinstated at 13b.29 as 'needless to say'
(entertained) R' Meir's 'and responds' in the middle is out of fear -- rejected at 13b.28 as needless, reinstated at 13b.29 as 'needless to say'

the mishnah is defective and teaches thus: R' Meir -- at the breaks greets out of respect and needless to say responds; in the middle greets out of fear and needless to say responds; R' Yehuda -- in the middle greets out of fear and responds out of respect, at the breaks greets out of respect and responds to anyone

מאי שנא מכאן ואילך מצות כוונה -- משום דכתיב על לבבכם? הכא נמי הא כתיב על לבבך! -- if intent is the mitzva only from 'upon your heart' on because the second paragraph says 'upon your hearts', the first paragraph has 'upon your heart' too
הכי קאמר: עד כאן מצות קריאה וכוונה, מכאן ואילך כוונה בלא קריאה -- intent runs throughout; what changes at 'upon your heart' is that recitation stops (= p_ry_reading)
this is what R' Yoshiya means: to here the mitzva of recitation AND intent; from here on, intent without recitation
ומאי שנא עד כאן מצות קריאה וכוונה -- דכתיב על לבבך ודברת בם? התם נמי הא כתיב על לבבכם לדבר בם! -- the second paragraph too has 'to speak of them', so recitation should be required there as well

ההוא בדברי תורה כתיב, והכי קאמר רחמנא: אגמירו בנייכו תורה כי היכי דליגרסו בהו -- 'to speak of them' in the second paragraph is written of Torah study (teach your children Torah so they are fluent), not of the Shema's recitation (= p_ledaber_bam_divrei_torah, p_agmiru_bnaichu_torah)
that verse ('to speak of them') is written of Torah study [not of the Shema's recitation]
R' Meir: 'Hear, Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One' -- to here intent of the heart is required
Sumchos: whoever prolongs [the word] 'echad', his days and years are prolonged for him
once you have crowned Him above and below and to the four winds of heaven, you need no more [prolonging]
